gloss: A large glossy purple vegetable with soft flesh, used in moussaka and curries.
usage: The standard word in UK shops, menus and recipes.
pitfall: Indian English 'brinjal' is understood by some but sounds unfamiliar to most Britons.
examples: Could you pick up two aubergines for the moussaka?
The roasted aubergine was the best thing on the menu.

gloss: A small green summer squash, eaten cooked or raw.
usage: The everyday British word in supermarkets, recipes and menus.
pragmatic_note: If you leave a courgette to grow huge, Britons call it a marrow.
pitfall: Americans say 'zucchini', which many Britons recognise but rarely use.
examples: Slice the courgettes thinly and fry them in olive oil.
We've got far too many courgettes from the allotment.

gloss: A fragrant herb; in the UK the word covers both the fresh leaves and the seeds.
usage: Used in recipes, shops and restaurants for the fresh leaves and the dried seeds alike.
pitfall: In the US 'coriander' usually means only the seeds; the leaves are 'cilantro'.
examples: Scatter some fresh coriander over the curry before serving.
I can't stand coriander; it tastes like soap to me.

gloss: A peppery salad leaf, often served with Parmesan or on pizza.
usage: Standard on British menus and supermarket salad bags.
pitfall: 'Arugula' is the American word and sounds foreign in a UK shop.
examples: The pizza comes topped with rocket and Parmesan.
Could I have a rocket salad on the side, please?

gloss: Flat pea pods eaten whole, usually lightly stir-fried or steamed.
usage: Common in British supermarkets and recipes; borrowed from French 'eat all'.
pitfall: Pronounced 'monzh-TOO' in Britain; the final 't' is silent.
examples: Stir-fry the mangetout for just a minute or two.
This pack of mangetout is from Kenya.

gloss: A large root vegetable with yellow-orange flesh, often mashed.
usage: Common in winter cooking in England and Wales; in Scotland it is called 'neeps'.
pragmatic_note: In parts of northern England and Scotland people may call it a turnip.
examples: Mash the swede with plenty of butter and black pepper.
Haggis is traditionally served with mashed swede and potato.

gloss: A young onion with a small white bulb and long green leaves.
usage: The standard British term in shops and recipes.
examples: Finely slice two spring onions for the garnish.
Can you add spring onions to the shopping list?

gloss: A dark red root vegetable, often sold cooked and eaten in salads.
usage: The usual British word; 'beet' alone sounds American.
pragmatic_note: Britons often buy beetroot pre-cooked or pickled in jars.
examples: The beetroot has stained my fingers bright pink.
There's goat's cheese and beetroot salad to start.

gloss: Large flat pale-green beans that grow in thick pods.
usage: The usual UK name in recipes and on allotments.
examples: We grew broad beans on the allotment this year.
Pod the broad beans and blanch them briefly.

gloss: Thin green bean pods eaten whole after boiling or steaming.
usage: Common in UK shops; 'green beans' is also widely used.
examples: Serve the salmon with new potatoes and French beans.
Top and tail the French beans before you cook them.

gloss: The sweet yellow kernels of maize, eaten as a vegetable.
usage: Standard UK word on tins, menus and pizza toppings.
pitfall: In Britain 'corn' alone can mean any cereal crop, so say 'sweetcorn' for the vegetable.
examples: Would you like sweetcorn on your jacket potato?
Drain a tin of sweetcorn and stir it in.

gloss: A Chinese cabbage with white stalks and dark green leaves.
usage: The spelling and name used in British supermarkets and recipes.
examples: Steam the pak choi and drizzle it with soy sauce.
Baby pak choi is lovely in a noodle soup.

gloss: A hollow, sweet vegetable in red, green, yellow or orange; also called a sweet pepper.
usage: Britons say 'a red pepper' or 'a green pepper' in shops and recipes.
pitfall: Indian English 'capsicum' is rarely used in Britain; 'bell pepper' sounds American.
examples: Chop one red pepper and one onion.
Stuffed peppers are on the menu tonight.

gloss: A small hot pepper, or a spicy stew made with it.
usage: British spelling is 'chilli' with two Ls, for both the pepper and the dish.
pitfall: Spelling 'chili' looks American; 'chilli con carne' is the UK menu spelling.
examples: Go easy on the chilli; the kids won't eat it.
We're having chilli con carne for tea.

gloss: A very large, mild-tasting green squash, like an overgrown courgette.
usage: Associated with British vegetable gardens and village shows.
pragmatic_note: Growing the biggest marrow is a classic competition at British village fêtes.
pitfall: Not to be confused with bone marrow, which is also eaten.
examples: He won first prize for his marrow at the village show.
Stuffed marrow was a staple of my gran's cooking.

gloss: A tall lettuce with long crisp leaves, used in Caesar salad.
usage: Standard UK name in shops; 'romaine' is increasingly seen too.
examples: A Caesar salad really needs crisp cos lettuce.
Grab a cos lettuce and some tomatoes, please.

gloss: Pale dried seedless grapes, used in cakes, scones and cereal.
usage: Very common in British baking; distinguished from darker raisins and smaller currants.
examples: Do you want plain scones or ones with sultanas?
Soak the sultanas in tea overnight for the fruit loaf.

gloss: A small, sweet, easy-peeling citrus fruit, popular at Christmas.
usage: The everyday British word for most small easy-peel oranges.
pragmatic_note: A satsuma in the toe of a Christmas stocking is a long-standing British tradition.
examples: There's a satsuma in the bottom of every stocking.
I've packed you a satsuma for your break.

gloss: An informal word for a potato.
usage: Friendly, everyday British word, common in conversation and cheerful menus.
examples: Can you peel the spuds while I do the gravy?
Nothing beats a baked spud on a cold day.

gloss: Short for vegetables, used as a singular or plural noun.
usage: Extremely common in everyday British speech and on menus.
pragmatic_note: 'Meat and two veg' describes a traditional, plain British dinner.
pitfall: Britons say 'veg' where Americans say 'veggies'; 'veggie' in the UK usually means vegetarian.
examples: Make sure you eat your veg.
It's a proper meat-and-two-veg kind of place.

gloss: The single hard seed in the middle of fruit such as cherries, plums or peaches.
usage: Standard British word in recipes and on packaging ('may contain stones').
pitfall: Saying 'pit' sounds American; Britons 'stone' cherries rather than 'pit' them.
examples: Careful, the olives still have their stones in.
Halve the plums and remove the stones.

gloss: Ordinary wheat flour with no raising agent added.
usage: Standard term in British recipes and on supermarket shelves.
pitfall: Do not swap it for self-raising flour, or your sauce or pastry will behave differently.
examples: You'll need 200 grams of plain flour.
Dust the worktop with a little plain flour.

gloss: Flour with baking powder already mixed in, used for cakes and scones.
usage: A staple in British kitchens and in almost every classic sponge recipe.
pitfall: Note the UK spelling 'raising' rather than the American 'rising'.
examples: Use self-raising flour, or add baking powder to plain.
We've run out of self-raising flour.

gloss: Made from the whole grain of wheat, including the bran.
usage: Standard British word for bread and flour; 'brown bread' is also common.
pitfall: 'Whole wheat' is American; 'wholegrain' is used in the UK too, but for a broader category.
examples: Could I have that on wholemeal bread, please?
Wholemeal pasta keeps you fuller for longer.

gloss: Very fine white sugar that dissolves quickly, used in baking and meringues.
usage: Found in almost every British cake recipe.
pitfall: Not the same as icing sugar, which is a powder.
examples: Beat the butter and caster sugar until pale and fluffy.
Sprinkle a little caster sugar over the strawberries.

gloss: Sugar ground to a fine powder, used for icing and dusting cakes.
usage: Standard British term in recipes and on packets.
examples: Dust the cake with icing sugar just before serving.
Mix the icing sugar with a little lemon juice.

gloss: A sweet coating or decoration for cakes, made mainly from sugar.
usage: The usual British word for any cake topping, including buttercream.
pitfall: 'Frosting' is understood but sounds American; Britons 'ice' a cake.
examples: Wait until the cake has cooled before you add the icing.
She's piped the icing beautifully.

gloss: A thick, golden, sweet syrup made from sugar refining, used in baking.
usage: A classic British store-cupboard item for flapjacks, treacle tart and porridge.
pitfall: Corn syrup is not quite the same; British recipes rely on golden syrup's flavour.
examples: Warm the golden syrup with the butter for the flapjacks.
I like a spoonful of golden syrup on my porridge.

gloss: A thick dark sugar syrup; 'black treacle' is close to American molasses.
usage: Used in traditional British baking such as parkin and treacle toffee.
pragmatic_note: Despite the name, treacle tart is made with golden syrup, not black treacle.
examples: Parkin gets its dark colour from black treacle.
Add a tablespoon of treacle to the gingerbread.

gloss: A white powder used as a raising agent in baking.
usage: Common in British recipes, often shortened to 'bicarb'.
pitfall: It is not the same as baking powder, though both help cakes rise.
examples: Add half a teaspoon of bicarbonate of soda.
Have we got any bicarb left?

gloss: A fine white starch from maize, used to thicken sauces.
usage: Standard term in British recipes and shops.
pitfall: In the US 'corn flour' can mean finely ground cornmeal, which is different.
examples: Thicken the sauce with a teaspoon of cornflour.
Mix the cornflour with a little cold water first.

gloss: Tiny coloured sugar balls or strands scattered over cakes and desserts.
usage: A nostalgic British term, especially for children's party food.
examples: The kids want hundreds and thousands on their fairy cakes.
Top the trifle with a few hundreds and thousands.

gloss: A small cube of dried, concentrated stock, dissolved in hot water.
usage: A standard item in British kitchens and recipes.
examples: Crumble a chicken stock cube into the boiling water.
We need vegetable stock cubes for the soup.

gloss: A thick, concentrated tomato paste sold in tubes or tins.
usage: Standard UK term on packaging and in recipes.
pitfall: In Britain this is the thick paste; American 'tomato puree' is thinner, closer to passata.
examples: Squeeze in a tablespoon of tomato purée.
We're nearly out of tomato purée.

gloss: Smooth, uncooked sieved tomatoes, sold in jars or cartons.
usage: Very common in British supermarkets and pasta recipes.
pitfall: Do not confuse with British 'tomato purée', which is a thick paste.
examples: Pour in a carton of passata and simmer.
Passata makes a quick pizza sauce.

gloss: A light cooking oil pressed from the seeds of the yellow rapeseed plant.
usage: Widely sold in British supermarkets; often British-grown.
pragmatic_note: The bright yellow fields seen across the British countryside in spring are rapeseed.
examples: Cold-pressed rapeseed oil is great for roast potatoes.
Fry the onions in a little rapeseed oil.

gloss: Thin pouring cream with a lower fat content, used in coffee and over desserts.
usage: Standard British supermarket label.
pitfall: Single cream cannot be whipped; you need double cream for that.
examples: Would you like single cream with your crumble?
Add a splash of single cream to the soup.

gloss: Thick, rich cream that can be whipped or poured over puddings.
usage: Standard British supermarket label and recipe ingredient.
examples: Whip the double cream until it forms soft peaks.
Pour a little double cream over the apple pie.

gloss: Very thick, rich, yellowish cream from Devon and Cornwall, eaten with scones.
usage: Essential to a cream tea in the West Country and in tearooms nationwide.
pragmatic_note: Devon and Cornwall famously disagree on whether cream or jam goes on the scone first.
examples: The scones come with strawberry jam and clotted cream.
Clotted cream ice cream is a Cornish treat.

gloss: Milk with about half the fat removed; the most popular milk in Britain.
usage: Used in shops and cafés; colour-coded caps help shoppers (often green).
examples: Can you get two pints of semi-skimmed?
Is that semi-skimmed or full-fat?

gloss: Describes milk or dairy products with none of the fat removed.
usage: Standard British label: 'full-fat milk', 'full-fat yoghurt'.
pitfall: Britons rarely say 'whole milk' in shops, though it appears on some labels.
examples: The baby's on full-fat milk now.
Use full-fat yoghurt or the sauce might split.

gloss: A thick, slightly sour food made from fermented milk.
usage: Usual British spelling, pronounced 'YOG-urt' with a short 'o'.
pitfall: Americans say 'YOH-gurt'; 'natural yoghurt' in the UK means plain yogurt.
examples: I'll just have yoghurt and fruit for breakfast.
A spoonful of natural yoghurt cools the curry down.

gloss: Meat, usually beef, finely chopped by machine; also 'minced beef'.
usage: The standard British word on butchers' counters and in recipes.
pitfall: Saying 'ground beef' sounds American; in Scotland 'mince and tatties' is a classic dish.
examples: Pick up 500 grams of beef mince for the lasagne.
Brown the mince in batches.

gloss: Bacon from the pork belly, with stripes of fat; the standard American kind.
usage: A common British supermarket choice, often for wrapping or crisping.
pitfall: In Britain plain 'bacon' usually means back bacon, not streaky.
examples: Wrap each chicken breast in streaky bacon.
I prefer crispy streaky bacon in my BLT.

gloss: Lean bacon cut from the pork loin, with a strip of fat on one side.
usage: The default bacon in a British fry-up or bacon sandwich.
examples: Two rashers of back bacon, please.
The full English comes with back bacon and sausage.

gloss: A single thin slice of bacon.
usage: The everyday British word for a slice of bacon.
examples: How many rashers do you want?
Grill four rashers of bacon until crisp.

gloss: Cured pork leg, cooked as a thick steak or a whole joint.
usage: Classic pub menu item ('gammon, egg and chips') and Christmas joint.
pragmatic_note: 'Gammon steak with pineapple' is a retro pub-menu favourite.
pitfall: Britons call it 'ham' once it has been cooked and is served cold.
examples: I'll have the gammon with egg and chips.
We're glazing a gammon joint for Boxing Day.

gloss: A large piece of meat for roasting, such as beef, lamb or pork.
usage: Standard British word for the centrepiece of a Sunday roast.
pitfall: In this sense it has nothing to do with body joints or slang meanings.
examples: We'll get a joint of beef for Sunday.
Let the joint rest before you carve it.

gloss: A boneless cut of meat or fish.
usage: Pronounced 'FILL-it' in Britain, with the final 't' sounded.
pitfall: Americans say 'fil-AY'; the British pronunciation sounds the 't'.
examples: I'll have the fillet steak, medium rare.
Season the salmon fillets on both sides.

gloss: A small, thin pork sausage.
usage: Common in Britain at Christmas, wrapped in bacon as 'pigs in blankets'.
examples: Wrap the chipolatas in streaky bacon.
The kids always eat all the chipolatas first.

gloss: An informal British word for a sausage.
usage: Friendly, everyday word, famous in 'bangers and mash'.
pitfall: Also slang for an old car, but in food contexts it always means sausage.
examples: Shall we stick some bangers on the barbecue?
These are proper butcher's bangers.

gloss: A dark sausage made from pork blood, fat and oatmeal, sliced and fried.
usage: A traditional part of a full breakfast, especially in the north and Scotland.
pragmatic_note: Bury in Lancashire and Stornoway in Scotland are famous for it.
pitfall: Despite the name, it is not a dessert.
examples: Would you like black pudding with your breakfast?
Black pudding is surprisingly good with scallops.

gloss: Crunchy deep-fried pieces of pork skin and fat, sold in packets in pubs.
usage: A classic British pub snack, eaten with a pint.
examples: Do you want crisps or pork scratchings?
He always orders a pint and a bag of pork scratchings.

gloss: The crisp, salty roasted skin on a joint of pork.
usage: A prized part of a British roast pork dinner.
pragmatic_note: Getting good crackling is a point of pride for British home cooks.
examples: Score the skin well if you want good crackling.
Who gets the last bit of crackling?

gloss: Hard fat from around the kidneys of cattle or sheep, used in puddings and dumplings.
usage: A key ingredient in traditional British puddings, pastry and dumplings.
examples: Suet pastry gives the pie its soft, rich crust.
You can buy vegetable suet for vegetarians.

gloss: Small shellfish; 'prawn' is the general British word.
usage: Standard in British shops and menus; 'shrimp' is used only for very small ones.
pitfall: American 'shrimp' covers sizes Britons call prawns or king prawns.
examples: I'll have the garlic king prawns to start.
A prawn sandwich is a lunchtime classic.

gloss: Breaded and fried langoustine tails, served with chips and tartare sauce.
usage: A familiar British pub-menu dish, 'scampi and chips'.
pitfall: In Britain it means the breaded seafood, not the Italian-American garlic shrimp dish.
examples: I'll have scampi and chips, please.
Scampi comes with tartare sauce and a wedge of lemon.

gloss: Rectangular strips of white fish coated in breadcrumbs.
usage: A British freezer staple and children's favourite.
pragmatic_note: A fish finger sandwich is a nostalgic British comfort food.
examples: The kids want fish fingers, chips and beans.
A fish finger sandwich with ketchup is pure comfort food.

gloss: A whole herring, split, salted and smoked, often eaten for breakfast.
usage: Traditional British breakfast food, now somewhat old-fashioned.
examples: Grandad always has kippers on a Sunday morning.
The hotel serves grilled kippers at breakfast.

gloss: Small sugary treats such as toffees, gums and boiled sweets.
usage: The everyday British word; 'candy' sounds American.
pitfall: In Britain 'a sweet' can also mean the dessert course in some households.
examples: Don't eat all those sweets before dinner.
We bought a bag of sweets for the car journey.

gloss: Loose sweets that you choose yourself and pay for by weight or bag.
usage: A nostalgic British treat, found at cinemas and sweet shops.
examples: Let's get some pick 'n' mix for the film.
The cinema still has a pick 'n' mix stand.

gloss: A hard stick of brightly coloured sugar sold at British seaside resorts.
usage: Classic souvenir from seaside towns such as Blackpool and Brighton.
pragmatic_note: Seaside rock traditionally has the resort's name running right through it.
examples: We brought back a stick of rock from Blackpool.
The name runs all the way through the rock.

gloss: Spun sugar served as a fluffy cloud on a stick.
usage: Sold at British funfairs, piers and seaside resorts.
examples: The kids want candyfloss on the pier.
Candyfloss always makes my hands sticky.

gloss: An apple on a stick coated in hard toffee.
usage: Traditional around Bonfire Night and at autumn funfairs.
examples: We always had toffee apples on Bonfire Night.
Careful, toffee apples are murder on your teeth.

gloss: Frozen flavoured water or juice on a stick.
usage: Everyday British word; often shortened to 'lolly'.
pitfall: In Britain a 'lolly' can mean a lollipop or an ice lolly depending on context.
examples: It's boiling; shall we get an ice lolly?
The kids are eating ice lollies in the garden.

gloss: A soft-serve ice cream cone with a chocolate flake pushed into it.
usage: A British ice-cream-van classic, said 'ninety-nine'.
pragmatic_note: Nobody agrees on why it is called a 99; it is simply part of a British summer.
examples: Can I have a 99 with strawberry sauce?
Nothing says summer like a 99 from the van.

gloss: A fizzy, sweet, flavoured powder eaten as a sweet.
usage: A traditional British children's sweet, often in a 'sherbet dip'.
pitfall: In the US 'sherbet' is a fruity frozen dessert; in Britain it is a fizzy powder.
examples: We used to buy sherbet dips from the corner shop.
Lemon sherbets are my favourite sweets.

gloss: Chewy, firm fruit-flavoured sweets, despite the name containing no wine.
usage: A long-standing British sweet, popular on car journeys.
pitfall: They contain no alcohol, so they are fine for children and non-drinkers.
examples: Pass me the wine gums, would you?
Wine gums don't actually contain any wine.

gloss: A small, flat, usually crisp baked treat, often dunked in tea.
usage: Universal British word; 'cookie' is used only for large, chewy American-style ones.
pragmatic_note: Offering a biscuit with a cup of tea is basic British hospitality.
pitfall: In the US a 'biscuit' is a soft savoury bread roll, closer to a British scone.
examples: Would you like a biscuit with your tea?
Who's eaten all the chocolate biscuits?

gloss: A semi-sweet wholemeal biscuit, plain or coated in chocolate.
usage: Probably Britain's best-known biscuit, also used for cheesecake bases.
examples: Crush some digestives for the cheesecake base.
A chocolate digestive with a cup of tea is perfect.

gloss: A biscuit sandwich with a vanilla cream filling.
usage: One of Britain's favourite everyday biscuits.
pitfall: There is no actual custard inside.
examples: Pass the custard creams, please.
Custard creams are always the first to go.

gloss: A chocolate biscuit sandwich with chocolate cream filling.
usage: A familiar British biscuit, found in most biscuit tins.
pitfall: In the biscuit aisle it has nothing to do with whiskey.
examples: Do you prefer bourbons or custard creams?
I always eat the cream out of a bourbon first.

gloss: A rich, crumbly Scottish biscuit made from butter, sugar and flour.
usage: Associated with Scotland, Christmas tins and afternoon tea.
examples: We brought back a tin of shortbread from Edinburgh.
Homemade shortbread only needs three ingredients.

gloss: A chewy baked bar made from oats, butter, sugar and golden syrup.
usage: A staple of British cafés, bake sales and lunchboxes.
pitfall: In the US a 'flapjack' is a pancake.
examples: I'll have a coffee and a flapjack, please.
Flapjacks are the easiest thing to bake for a bake sale.

gloss: A small sponge disc topped with orange jelly and chocolate.
usage: An iconic British snack; the name is used generically for supermarket versions too.
pragmatic_note: Britons love arguing whether it is a cake or a biscuit; a court once ruled it a cake.
examples: Is a Jaffa Cake a cake or a biscuit?
I could eat a whole packet of Jaffa Cakes.

gloss: To dip a biscuit briefly into tea or coffee before eating it.
usage: A cherished British habit; everyone has a view on the best biscuit for dunking.
pragmatic_note: Losing half a biscuit in your tea is a small, very British tragedy.
pitfall: In basketball contexts it means something else entirely.
examples: Do you dunk your biscuits?
I dunked it too long and it fell in my tea.

gloss: A selection of cheeses served with savoury crackers, often after a meal.
usage: Served at the end of a dinner party or at Christmas.
pragmatic_note: Offering cheese and biscuits after pudding is a traditional British dinner-party touch.
pitfall: The 'biscuits' here are savoury crackers, not sweet biscuits.
examples: Shall we have cheese and biscuits instead of pudding?
There's port, cheese and biscuits after dinner.

gloss: A small, lightly sweet baked bread, split and eaten with butter, jam and cream.
usage: Central to a British cream tea; also sold plain, fruit or cheese.
pragmatic_note: Britons argue over whether it rhymes with 'gone' or 'bone'; both are correct.
pitfall: An American 'scone' is often sweeter and triangular; British scones are round and plainer.
examples: Would you like a scone with jam and cream?
These cheese scones are still warm.

gloss: A soft, round griddle cake full of holes, toasted and eaten with butter.
usage: A British teatime and breakfast favourite, especially in winter.
pitfall: Different from an English muffin, which is a smoother bread roll.
examples: Nothing beats a hot buttered crumpet in winter.
Shall I toast some crumpets?

gloss: Either a flat, round bread roll toasted for breakfast, or a sweet American-style cake.
usage: Both meanings are current in Britain; context usually makes it clear.
pitfall: Ask whether someone means an 'English muffin' or a 'blueberry muffin' if unclear.
examples: I'll have eggs Benedict on a toasted muffin.
They sell blueberry muffins at the station café.

gloss: A light, sweet yeasted bun with dried fruit, split, toasted and buttered.
usage: Traditional British café and teatime food; meaning varies by region.
pragmatic_note: In parts of northern England 'teacake' can simply mean a bread roll.
examples: A toasted teacake and a pot of tea, please.
The café does lovely toasted teacakes.

gloss: A spiced sweet bun with dried fruit and a cross on top, eaten at Easter.
usage: Traditionally eaten on Good Friday; now sold for weeks around Easter.
examples: We always have hot cross buns on Good Friday.
Toast the hot cross buns and butter them.

gloss: A light sponge cake sandwiched with jam and cream or buttercream.
usage: Britain's classic teatime cake, named after Queen Victoria.
examples: She's made a Victoria sponge for the village fête.
A slice of Victoria sponge with my tea, please.

gloss: A light, airy cake made with eggs, sugar, flour and butter.
usage: Common British shorthand in recipes, cafés and puddings.
examples: The sponge has sunk in the middle.
Treacle sponge and custard is a proper school pudding.

gloss: A small, light sponge cake baked in a paper case and iced.
usage: Traditional British name, especially for small, simple ones at children's parties.
pitfall: 'Cupcake' is also common in Britain now, usually for larger, heavily iced ones.
examples: We made fairy cakes for her birthday party.
Fairy cakes with hundreds and thousands are a childhood classic.

gloss: A thin sponge spread with jam or cream and rolled into a spiral.
usage: A familiar British supermarket and homemade cake.
pitfall: Despite the name, it is not specifically Swiss.
examples: Roll the Swiss roll while the sponge is still warm.
A chocolate Swiss roll makes a quick yule log.

gloss: A shortcrust tart with jam, almond sponge filling and flaked almonds or icing.
usage: A traditional English bake named after Bakewell in Derbyshire.
examples: The café's Bakewell tart is still warm.
Cherry Bakewells have a glacé cherry on top.

gloss: In Britain, a no-bake chocolate traybake with crushed biscuits and dried fruit.
usage: A popular café and bake-sale treat, especially in Scotland.
pitfall: In India 'tiffin' means a light meal or lunch box; in Britain it usually means this chocolate bake.
examples: They do a lovely chocolate tiffin at the café.
Tiffin is easy because you don't need to bake it.

gloss: A rich, dark fruit cake covered with marzipan and white icing.
usage: Made weeks before Christmas and 'fed' with brandy in many British homes.
examples: I've been feeding the Christmas cake with brandy for weeks.
Do you want a slice of Christmas cake?

gloss: A small sweet pie filled with mincemeat: dried fruit, spices and suet.
usage: Eaten throughout the British Christmas season, often warm with cream or brandy butter.
pitfall: Modern 'mincemeat' in a mince pie contains no meat.
examples: Have a mince pie and a mulled wine.
We leave a mince pie out for Father Christmas.

gloss: A small individual loaf of bread.
usage: Universal British term, but local names vary hugely by region.
pragmatic_note: Bap, barm, cob, bun and batch are all regional words for a roll, and Britons love to argue about them.
examples: Could I have a bread roll with my soup?
Grab a pack of bread rolls for the barbecue.

gloss: A large, soft, round bread roll.
usage: Common across much of Britain, especially for breakfast and burgers.
pragmatic_note: Regional: in the north-west a roll is often a 'barm' and in the Midlands a 'cob'.
examples: I'll have a bacon and egg bap, please.
Get some floury baps for the burgers.

gloss: A flat, oval bread that opens into a pocket.
usage: British spelling, pronounced 'PIT-uh' with a short 'i'.
pitfall: Americans spell it 'pita' and say 'PEE-tuh'.
examples: Warm the pittas and fill them with falafel.
Serve the hummus with toasted pitta bread.

gloss: The sweet course of a meal, or a specific baked or steamed sweet dish.
usage: Very common in British homes and restaurants for the dessert course.
pragmatic_note: Some Britons consider 'pudding' less formal or more upper-class than 'dessert'; both are fine.
pitfall: American 'pudding' usually means a creamy custard-like dessert; British puddings can even be savoury.
examples: What's for pudding?
I'm too full for pudding, thanks.

gloss: An informal British word for the dessert course.
usage: Used casually at home, especially in the north and among older speakers.
examples: Is there anything for afters?
Eat your veg or there's no afters.

gloss: The dessert course of a meal.
usage: Used in some British households and older menus: 'Would you like a sweet?'
pragmatic_note: Word choice for the dessert course (pudding, sweet, dessert, afters) carries subtle class signals in Britain.
examples: Would anyone like a sweet?
There's a choice of sweet on the set menu.

gloss: A sweet, pourable yellow sauce made from milk, eggs or custard powder.
usage: The classic British accompaniment to crumbles, pies and steamed puddings.
pitfall: British custard is usually a hot pouring sauce, not the set American custard.
examples: Would you like custard or cream with your crumble?
Apple pie and custard is my idea of heaven.

gloss: A wobbly, fruit-flavoured dessert set with gelatine.
usage: A British children's party favourite, often served with ice cream.
pitfall: American 'jelly' is a fruit spread; Britons call that jam.
examples: We're having jelly and ice cream at the party.
Put the jelly in the fridge to set.

gloss: A thick, sweet spread made from fruit boiled with sugar.
usage: The normal British word for any fruit spread except citrus marmalade.
pitfall: Britons say 'jam sandwich' where Americans say 'jelly sandwich'.
examples: Would you like jam or marmalade on your toast?
Strawberry jam and clotted cream on a scone is perfect.

gloss: A bitter-sweet preserve made from citrus fruit, usually Seville oranges.
usage: A classic British breakfast spread on toast.
pitfall: In Britain 'marmalade' means citrus only; in other languages it can mean any jam.
examples: Toast and marmalade is all I need in the morning.
Seville oranges are in season for marmalade-making.

gloss: Baked fruit topped with a crumbly mix of flour, butter and sugar.
usage: One of Britain's favourite home-made puddings, almost always with custard.
examples: Apple and blackberry crumble is perfect in autumn.
Rhubarb crumble and custard, please.

gloss: Layers of sponge, fruit or jelly, custard and cream in a glass bowl.
usage: A traditional British party and Christmas dessert.
pitfall: 'A trifle' also means 'slightly', as in 'a trifle cold', which is unrelated.
examples: Nan makes a sherry trifle every Christmas.
Who wants a bowl of trifle?

gloss: A dessert of crushed meringue, whipped cream and strawberries.
usage: A popular British summer pudding, linked to Eton College.
examples: Eton mess is the easiest summer pudding.
Fold the strawberries through the cream for the Eton mess.

gloss: A moist date sponge covered in hot toffee sauce.
usage: A favourite on British pub and restaurant pudding menus.
examples: I'll have the sticky toffee pudding with ice cream.
Their sticky toffee pudding is legendary.

gloss: Buttered bread layered with dried fruit and baked in egg custard.
usage: Traditional British comfort food, a thrifty way to use stale bread.
pitfall: In Britain 'bread pudding' is a different, denser cake-like bake.
examples: Bread and butter pudding is the best use of stale bread.
Mum's bread and butter pudding is the best.

gloss: A dark, rich steamed pudding of dried fruit and spices, served at Christmas.
usage: Served after Christmas dinner in Britain, often set alight with brandy.
pragmatic_note: Families traditionally stir the mixture and make a wish on 'Stir-up Sunday'.
examples: Pour warm brandy over the Christmas pudding and light it.
Do you want brandy butter or custard with your pudding?

gloss: Thick-cut strips of potato, deep-fried, as in fish and chips.
usage: Everyday word in shops, pubs and restaurants; a 'chippy' is a fish-and-chip shop.
pragmatic_note: Thin American-style fries are often still called 'fries' in the UK, especially at fast-food chains.
pitfall: In the US 'chips' means what Britons call crisps.
examples: Shall we grab fish and chips on the way home?
Do you want salt and vinegar on your chips?

gloss: Thin slices of potato fried until crunchy, sold in packets.
usage: Universal British word; a packet of crisps is a standard lunchbox and pub snack.
pragmatic_note: Britons buy crisps in single 'packets', and multipacks for lunchboxes.
pitfall: Asking for 'chips' in a UK shop will get you hot chips, not crisps.
examples: Could I have a packet of crisps with that?
Cheese and onion crisps are my weakness.

gloss: The classic seasoning for chips, and a popular crisp flavour.
usage: Asked as standard in British chip shops: 'Salt and vinegar?'
pitfall: British chip shops use malt vinegar, which tastes different from white vinegar.
examples: Salt and vinegar on your chips, love?
Salt and vinegar crisps make my mouth sting.

gloss: A whole potato baked in its skin and filled with toppings.
usage: Common in British cafés, pubs and canteens as a lunchtime option.
pitfall: 'Baked potato' is also understood in the UK; 'jacket' refers to the skin.
examples: I'll have a jacket potato with cheese and beans.
Jacket potatoes take about an hour in the oven.

gloss: Potatoes boiled and crushed with butter and milk until smooth.
usage: The usual British word on menus and at home.
pitfall: Britons treat 'mash' as uncountable: 'some mash', not 'some mashes'.
examples: Sausages and mash for tea tonight.
Could I swap the chips for mash?

gloss: Potatoes parboiled then roasted in hot fat until crisp outside and fluffy inside.
usage: An essential part of a British Sunday roast or Christmas dinner.
pragmatic_note: Many Britons think their own roast potatoes are the best, and say so.
pitfall: Not the same as American 'roasted potatoes', which are usually chunks tossed in oil.
examples: The secret to good roast potatoes is goose fat.
Can I have more roast potatoes, please?

gloss: Soft, mashed marrowfat peas, served with fish and chips.
usage: A chip-shop classic, especially in the north of England.
examples: Fish, chips and mushy peas, please.
Mushy peas are an acquired taste for some visitors.

gloss: A cooked breakfast of bacon, sausages, eggs, beans, tomatoes, mushrooms and toast.
usage: Served in British cafés, hotels and pubs; regional versions include the full Scottish and Ulster fry.
pragmatic_note: Ordering a full English at a weekend is a British ritual, especially after a late night.
examples: I'll have the full English with extra toast.
Nothing cures a hangover like a full English.

gloss: An informal word for a cooked breakfast of fried foods.
usage: Common in everyday British speech, especially at weekends.
examples: Fancy a fry-up on Saturday morning?
The café does a cracking fry-up.

gloss: Baked beans in tomato sauce, heated and poured over buttered toast.
usage: A quick, cheap British meal, classic for students and lazy evenings.
examples: I'm just having beans on toast tonight.
Beans on toast with grated cheese is the best version.

gloss: Cheese melted on toast under the grill.
usage: A simple British snack or light supper.
pitfall: It is made open, under the grill, unlike an American grilled cheese sandwich.
examples: I'll just make myself some cheese on toast.
A dash of Worcestershire sauce on cheese on toast is lovely.

gloss: Toast topped with a savoury sauce of cheese, mustard, ale and Worcestershire sauce, then grilled.
usage: A traditional British savoury, often on café and gastropub menus.
examples: The Welsh rarebit comes with a side salad.
Welsh rarebit is posh cheese on toast.

gloss: Thin strips of buttered toast for dipping into a soft-boiled egg.
usage: A classic British children's breakfast: 'egg and soldiers'.
examples: Do you want a boiled egg with soldiers?
Dip your soldiers in the yolk.

gloss: Fried leftover potatoes and vegetables, especially cabbage, from a roast dinner.
usage: Traditional British dish, often eaten on Boxing Day or with a fry-up.
examples: We'll have bubble and squeak with the leftovers.
Bubble and squeak goes well with a fried egg.

gloss: Oats cooked in milk or water, eaten hot for breakfast.
usage: The usual British word, especially associated with Scotland.
pitfall: In Britain 'oatmeal' means the ground oats themselves, not the cooked dish.
examples: I have porridge with honey every morning.
Porridge keeps me going until lunch.

gloss: A dish of rice, smoked fish, hard-boiled eggs and curry spices.
usage: An Anglo-Indian dish that became a British country-house breakfast; now rather traditional.
pragmatic_note: Its name comes from the Indian dish khichdi, which is quite different.
examples: The hotel serves kedgeree at breakfast.
Kedgeree is a great way to use smoked haddock.

gloss: A very informal word for a sandwich.
usage: Common in casual British speech, especially in the north.
pitfall: Fine among friends, but say 'sandwich' in formal or work emails.
examples: I've made you a cheese sarnie for later.
Fancy a bacon sarnie?

gloss: An informal northern English word for a sandwich, especially a hot one.
usage: Typical in northern England; heard nationwide in fixed phrases like 'bacon butty'.
pragmatic_note: Strongly associated with Lancashire, Merseyside and Yorkshire speech.
examples: I'll have a sausage butty and a brew.
There's nothing like a butty on a cold morning.

gloss: A sandwich filled with hot bacon, often with brown or tomato sauce.
usage: A classic British café and breakfast food.
pragmatic_note: Whether a bacon butty needs brown sauce or ketchup is a serious British debate.
examples: A bacon butty with brown sauce, please.
Builders love a bacon butty for breakfast.

gloss: A soft white roll or bread filled with hot chips.
usage: A beloved, carb-heavy chip-shop staple in northern England.
examples: A chip butty is the ultimate comfort food.
I'll have a chip butty with plenty of vinegar.

gloss: A toasted sandwich, often filled with cheese and ham.
usage: Very common in British cafés and homes; made in a sandwich toaster or pan.
examples: I'll have a cheese and ham toastie, please.
A toastie and soup is perfect for lunch.

gloss: A cold meal of cheese, bread, pickle, salad and often ham or a pork pie.
usage: A traditional British pub lunch, often shortened to 'a ploughman's'.
pitfall: Note the British spelling 'plough', not 'plow'.
examples: I'll have a ploughman's and a half of cider.
The ploughman's comes with Cheddar, pickle and crusty bread.

gloss: A hard- or soft-boiled egg wrapped in sausage meat, coated in breadcrumbs and fried.
usage: A British picnic and pub snack.
pitfall: It is not Scottish in origin, despite the name.
examples: We packed Scotch eggs for the picnic.
The pub does a gorgeous runny Scotch egg.

gloss: Sausage meat wrapped in flaky pastry and baked.
usage: Eaten everywhere in Britain, from bakeries to party buffets.
examples: I'll grab a sausage roll from the bakery.
There are mini sausage rolls on the buffet.

gloss: A raised pie of chopped pork and jelly in hot-water crust pastry, eaten cold.
usage: A traditional British picnic, buffet and pub food; Melton Mowbray is famous for it.
pitfall: 'Porky pies' is rhyming slang for lies; in food contexts it means the pie.
examples: A slice of pork pie with some pickle, please.
Melton Mowbray pork pies have protected status.

gloss: A pastry case folded around a savoury filling such as beef, potato and swede.
usage: Associated with Cornwall; sold in bakeries across Britain.
pitfall: Pronounced 'PASS-tee' with a short 'a'; 'PAY-stee' means pale and unhealthy-looking.
examples: I'll have a Cornish pasty and a cup of tea.
Pasties were made for Cornish miners to eat underground.

gloss: Battered, deep-fried white fish served with chips.
usage: Britain's best-known takeaway, traditionally eaten on a Friday or at the seaside.
pragmatic_note: Eating fish and chips out of the paper by the sea is a classic British treat.
examples: Shall we get fish and chips on Friday?
Cod and chips twice, please.

gloss: A traditional Sunday meal of roast meat, potatoes, vegetables, Yorkshire puddings and gravy.
usage: Eaten at home or in pubs, usually at Sunday lunchtime.
pragmatic_note: Being invited for a Sunday roast is a warm sign of friendship or family welcome.
examples: Come round for a Sunday roast this weekend.
The pub's Sunday roast is booked up weeks ahead.

gloss: A puffed, crisp batter pudding baked in hot fat, served with roast beef and gravy.
usage: An essential part of a British Sunday roast, often shortened to 'Yorkshires'.
pragmatic_note: Some families serve Yorkshire puddings with every roast, not just beef.
pitfall: It is savoury, not a dessert.
examples: The secret to good Yorkshire puddings is very hot oil.
Can I have extra Yorkshires?

gloss: Sausages baked in Yorkshire pudding batter, served with gravy.
usage: A traditional British family supper.
pitfall: There is no toad in it; the name is simply playful.
examples: We're having toad in the hole for tea.
Toad in the hole needs plenty of onion gravy.

gloss: Sausages served with mashed potato and onion gravy.
usage: A classic British pub meal and home supper.
examples: Bangers and mash with onion gravy, please.
Bangers and mash is the ultimate comfort food.

gloss: Minced lamb in gravy, topped with mashed potato and baked.
usage: A traditional British family dish, also common in pubs.
pitfall: Strictly, shepherd's pie is lamb; the beef version is cottage pie.
examples: Shepherd's pie is a great way to use leftover lamb.
We're having shepherd's pie tonight.

gloss: Minced beef in gravy, topped with mashed potato and baked.
usage: A traditional British family dish, the beef version of shepherd's pie.
pitfall: Many people mix up cottage and shepherd's pie; the meat is what differs.
examples: Cottage pie is made with beef, not lamb.
I'll make a big cottage pie for the freezer.

gloss: A pie filled with chunks of beef and kidney in thick gravy.
usage: A traditional British pub dish, often made with ale.
examples: The pub's steak and kidney pie comes with mash.
Steak and ale pie is the more popular version now.

gloss: A minced-beef pie with mashed potato and green parsley sauce called 'liquor'.
usage: A traditional working-class London dish, served in old-fashioned pie shops.
pitfall: The parsley sauce is called 'liquor' but contains no alcohol.
examples: Pie and mash with liquor, please.
There are still a few old pie and mash shops in the East End.

gloss: Lamb and onions slow-cooked under a topping of sliced potatoes.
usage: A traditional dish from Lancashire in north-west England.
examples: Lancashire hotpot is perfect on a cold night.
The hotpot needs a good three hours in the oven.

gloss: A slow-cooked stew made in the oven, or the heavy pot it is cooked in.
usage: Very common British word for a stew baked in the oven.
pitfall: An American 'casserole' is often a baked dish with a creamy or cheesy topping.
examples: I'll put a chicken casserole in the oven.
Brown the meat before it goes in the casserole.

gloss: A Scottish dish of sheep's offal, oatmeal, onion and spices, cooked in a casing.
usage: Scotland's national dish, especially eaten on Burns Night with neeps and tatties.
pragmatic_note: Visitors are often teased that haggis is a small Highland animal.
examples: We had haggis, neeps and tatties on Burns Night.
Vegetarian haggis is surprisingly tasty.

gloss: Cold cooked chicken in a creamy, mildly curried mayonnaise sauce.
usage: Created for the 1953 coronation; a staple sandwich filling and buffet dish.
pitfall: It is very mild and sweet, nothing like an Indian curry.
examples: A coronation chicken sandwich, please.
Coronation chicken is a classic at British buffets.

gloss: Grilled chicken pieces in a creamy, spiced tomato sauce.
usage: One of Britain's most popular curry-house dishes, widely seen as a British creation.
pragmatic_note: It was once famously called 'a true British national dish' by a Foreign Secretary.
examples: I'll have a chicken tikka masala and pilau rice.
Tikka masala is the nation's favourite curry.

gloss: Spiced meat sliced from a vertical rotating spit, served in pitta or flatbread.
usage: A classic late-night British takeaway after the pub.
pragmatic_note: A 'kebab after the pub' is a stereotypical British end to a night out.
examples: They grabbed a doner kebab on the way home.
Do you want chilli sauce on your doner?

gloss: Small sausages wrapped in streaky bacon and roasted, eaten at Christmas.
usage: An essential side dish of a British Christmas dinner.
pragmatic_note: Many Britons say pigs in blankets are the best part of Christmas dinner.
pitfall: In the US 'pigs in a blanket' are sausages wrapped in pastry.
examples: You can never have too many pigs in blankets.
Who's eaten all the pigs in blankets?

gloss: A dark, tangy, fruity sauce made with tamarind, vinegar and spices.
usage: A classic British condiment for bacon sandwiches and fry-ups.
pragmatic_note: People are fiercely loyal to either brown sauce or ketchup on a bacon sandwich.
examples: Brown sauce or red sauce on your bacon butty?
Pass the brown sauce, would you?

gloss: In everyday British speech, often simply means tomato ketchup.
usage: Common in homes and cafés; also called 'red sauce' or 'ketchup'.
pitfall: On a British menu it can also mean a cooked pasta sauce, so check the context.
examples: Do you want tomato sauce with your chips?
Can I have some tomato sauce for my sausage roll?

gloss: A pale yellow, tangy, mayonnaise-like dressing.
usage: A traditional British condiment, especially on salads and sandwiches.
pragmatic_note: Salad cream has a nostalgic, slightly retro feel for many Britons.
pitfall: It is thinner and sharper than mayonnaise.
examples: My dad still puts salad cream on everything.
Egg and salad cream sandwiches remind me of childhood.

gloss: A bright yellow pickle of chopped vegetables in a mustard and turmeric sauce.
usage: A traditional British relish, eaten with cold meats, cheese and pork pies.
examples: Ham, cheese and a dollop of piccalilli is perfect.
Piccalilli is lovely with a pork pie.

gloss: In Britain, often a sweet-sour brown chunky relish eaten with cheese.
usage: Common in sandwiches like 'cheese and pickle' and with a ploughman's lunch.
pitfall: An American 'pickle' is a pickled cucumber, which Britons call a gherkin.
examples: A cheese and pickle sandwich, please.
The ploughman's comes with Cheddar and pickle.

gloss: A small cucumber pickled in vinegar.
usage: The usual British word, found in burgers and jars.
pragmatic_note: London's tower at 30 St Mary Axe is nicknamed 'the Gherkin'.
pitfall: Asking for 'a pickle' in Britain may get you chutney rather than a gherkin.
examples: Can I have my burger without the gherkin?
There's a jar of gherkins in the fridge.

gloss: A sharp sauce of chopped mint leaves in vinegar and sugar, served with roast lamb.
usage: A traditional British accompaniment to lamb.
pitfall: It is thin and vinegary, not a sweet mint jelly.
examples: Roast lamb isn't the same without mint sauce.
Pass the mint sauce, please.

gloss: A thick white sauce of milk, breadcrumbs, onion and cloves, served with roast poultry.
usage: A traditional part of British Christmas dinner.
pragmatic_note: Bread sauce divides opinion; some families love it and others never serve it.
examples: Do you want bread sauce with your turkey?
Mum makes bread sauce every Christmas.

gloss: A very hot, bright yellow mustard, served with roast beef and ham.
usage: A traditional British condiment, much hotter than American mustard.
pitfall: Use it sparingly; it is far stronger than the mild yellow American kind.
examples: Careful, English mustard is really hot.
Ham sandwiches need a bit of English mustard.

gloss: A thin, dark, savoury sauce made with vinegar, anchovies and tamarind.
usage: Common in British cooking; pronounced 'WUSS-ter-sher'.
pitfall: Learners often over-pronounce it; Britons say about three syllables, 'WUSS-tuh-shuh'.
examples: Add a dash of Worcestershire sauce to the cheese on toast.
A Bloody Mary needs Worcestershire sauce.

gloss: A sticky, dark, salty yeast-extract spread, eaten thinly on toast.
usage: An iconic British spread; the name is also used to describe anything divisive.
pragmatic_note: Calling something 'a bit Marmite' means people either love it or hate it.
pitfall: Spread it very thinly; first-timers often use far too much.
examples: I love Marmite on hot buttered toast.
That film is a bit Marmite: you'll love it or hate it.

gloss: A firm cheese, originally from Cheddar in Somerset; Britain's most popular cheese.
usage: Sold by strength in Britain: mild, medium, mature, extra mature.
pitfall: British Cheddar is usually pale, not orange like some American versions.
examples: A mature Cheddar sandwich with pickle, please.
Grate some Cheddar over the top.

gloss: A rich, crumbly English blue cheese with protected status.
usage: A traditional British Christmas cheese, often eaten with port.
pitfall: Pronounced 'STIL-tun' with a weak second syllable.
examples: Stilton and port is a classic Christmas pairing.
Crumble some Stilton into the soup.

gloss: A mild, firm, orange-coloured English cheese.
usage: Common in British supermarkets; pronounced 'red LESS-ter'.
pitfall: 'Leicester' is pronounced 'LESS-ter', never 'LIE-sester'.
examples: Red Leicester melts beautifully on toast.
A cheese board with Red Leicester and Stilton.

gloss: A hard, mellow, orange English cheese from Gloucestershire.
usage: Traditional British cheese; pronounced 'double GLOSS-ter'.
pragmatic_note: It is famously used in the annual cheese-rolling race down Cooper's Hill.
pitfall: 'Gloucester' is pronounced 'GLOSS-ter'; the middle letters are silent.
examples: Double Gloucester is great in a cheese toastie.
They chase a wheel of Double Gloucester down the hill.

gloss: A light mid-morning snack, usually tea or coffee and a biscuit.
usage: A traditional, slightly old-fashioned but affectionate British term.
examples: Time for elevenses; who wants a cuppa?
We stopped for elevenses at a little café.

gloss: In much of northern England and Scotland, the main evening meal.
usage: Regional and class-linked: northerners often say 'tea' for the evening meal.
pragmatic_note: Saying 'What's for tea?' marks you as northern or working-class in some people's ears; neither is wrong.
pitfall: If invited 'for tea', check whether it means a cuppa or a full meal.
examples: What are we having for tea tonight?
Come round for your tea on Friday.

gloss: The main meal of the day; in some regions this means the midday meal.
usage: Most Britons use it for the evening meal, but many northerners mean lunch.
pragmatic_note: Lunch-dinner-tea versus lunch-dinner-supper usage is a classic British class and regional marker.
pitfall: School 'dinners' and 'dinner ladies' refer to lunch, not the evening meal.
examples: What time are we having dinner?
We're having a roast for dinner on Sunday.

gloss: An evening meal, often lighter or less formal; also a late snack before bed.
usage: Used across Britain; especially common among middle- and upper-class speakers.
pragmatic_note: Inviting friends 'for supper' sounds relaxed and informal compared with 'for dinner'.
examples: Come over for a kitchen supper on Saturday.
We had a light supper of soup and bread.

gloss: In Scotland, fish and chips; elsewhere, an evening meal of fish.
usage: Very common in Scottish chip shops: 'a fish supper' includes the chips.
examples: I'll have a fish supper and a can of juice.
Any chippy in Glasgow will do you a fish supper.

gloss: A light meal of sandwiches, scones and cakes with tea, served mid-afternoon.
usage: Taken in hotels and tearooms as a treat or celebration.
pragmatic_note: Afternoon tea is a special-occasion outing, not an everyday habit for most Britons.
pitfall: It is not the same as 'high tea', despite frequent confusion abroad.
examples: We're taking Mum for afternoon tea for her birthday.
Afternoon tea at the hotel comes on a three-tier stand.

gloss: Traditionally a substantial early-evening meal with tea, rather than an elegant snack.
usage: Now uncommon; historically a working-class evening meal.
pragmatic_note: Abroad 'high tea' sounds posh, but in Britain the elegant version is 'afternoon tea'.
pitfall: Hotels sometimes use 'high tea' for afternoon tea, which Britons may find odd.
examples: High tea was a hearty working-class meal.
Tourists often confuse high tea with afternoon tea.

gloss: Tea served with scones, clotted cream and jam.
usage: Especially associated with Devon and Cornwall, and offered in tearooms nationwide.
pragmatic_note: In Devon it's cream then jam; in Cornwall it's jam then cream, and people care.
examples: Let's stop for a cream tea in Devon.
A cream tea for two, please.

gloss: An informal word for breakfast.
usage: Used casually in British speech and on café chalkboards.
pitfall: Fine among friends; use 'breakfast' at work or in writing.
examples: What do you fancy for brekkie?
The café does an all-day brekkie.

gloss: A lunch of sandwiches and snacks prepared at home and taken to school or work.
usage: Standard British term; school children choose between packed lunch and school dinners.
examples: I'm taking a packed lunch to save money.
Do the kids want a packed lunch tomorrow?

gloss: The NHS-recommended five portions of fruit and vegetables daily.
usage: A well-known public-health guideline in Britain, often printed on food labels.
examples: This soup counts as two of your five a day.
Are you getting your five a day?

gloss: The day before Lent begins, when Britons traditionally eat pancakes.
usage: Commonly called 'Pancake Day'; some towns hold pancake races.
pragmatic_note: British pancakes are thin, like crêpes, often with lemon and sugar.
pitfall: Americans may know it as Mardi Gras, which to Britons suggests a carnival rather than pancakes.
examples: Are we having pancakes on Pancake Day?
Lemon and sugar is the classic Shrove Tuesday topping.

gloss: A cup of tea, informally.
usage: Extremely common and friendly British word, fine with colleagues.
pragmatic_note: Offering a cuppa is the default British gesture of welcome or comfort.
examples: Fancy a cuppa?
Let's sit down with a cuppa and sort it out.

gloss: Strong black tea made with a teabag, served with milk and often sugar.
usage: A common British way of describing a very strong, unfussy mug of tea.
examples: I'll have a builder's tea, two sugars.
She drinks it builder's: strong, milky and sweet.

gloss: An informal word for a cup of tea, especially in the north.
usage: Common in northern England: 'I'll put a brew on.'
pitfall: In Britain a 'brew' is usually tea; Americans may assume beer.
examples: Do you want a brew?
I'm gasping for a brew.

gloss: With milk added, describing tea or coffee.
usage: The usual way to say how you take your tea or coffee in Britain.
pragmatic_note: 'Milk and two sugars' or 'white, no sugar' is a normal British order.
pitfall: 'White coffee' in Britain simply means coffee with milk.
examples: How do you take it? White, no sugar, please.
Two white coffees and a tea, please.

gloss: A glass coffee pot with a plunger to press down the grounds.
usage: Common British word in homes and cafés.
pitfall: Pronounced 'caff-uh-TYAIR'; 'French press' is understood but less used.
examples: Shall I make a cafetière of coffee?
The café serves coffee in a cafetière for two.

gloss: Coffee made by pouring hot water through ground coffee in a paper filter.
usage: The standard British term for drip coffee.
examples: Is there any filter coffee on?
I prefer filter coffee to instant.

gloss: A concentrated fruit drink you dilute with water.
usage: A staple in British homes, especially for children: 'orange squash'.
pitfall: Not the vegetable or the sport; context makes it clear.
examples: Do you want some squash?
Don't make the squash too strong.

gloss: A sweet, concentrated fruit or flower drink diluted with water.
usage: Common British word, especially in 'elderflower cordial'.
pitfall: In the US 'cordial' can mean a sweet liqueur; British cordial is non-alcoholic.
examples: Elderflower cordial with sparkling water is lovely.
We make our own lime cordial.

gloss: A sweet, carbonated soft drink such as cola or lemonade.
usage: Standard British term; 'soft drink' and 'pop' are also used.
pragmatic_note: 'Pop' sounds northern or old-fashioned in much of Britain.
pitfall: 'Soda' in Britain often means soda water, not a sweet drink.
examples: The kids aren't allowed fizzy drinks at dinner.
Can I get you a fizzy drink?

gloss: In Britain, a clear, sweet, fizzy lemon-flavoured drink.
usage: Common in pubs, often mixed with beer or spirits.
pitfall: American lemonade is still and cloudy; ask for 'cloudy' or 'traditional lemonade' in Britain.
examples: A pint of lager with a splash of lemonade, please.
Can I have a lemonade with ice?

gloss: Ordinary water from the tap, served free in restaurants and pubs.
usage: Normal and polite to request in British restaurants and pubs.
pragmatic_note: Licensed premises in England, Scotland and Wales must provide free tap water on request.
pitfall: Asking for 'water' may get you charged for bottled water; say 'tap water'.
examples: Could we have a jug of tap water, please?
Just tap water for me, thanks.

gloss: A measure of 568 ml, the standard serving of beer or cider in British pubs.
usage: Universal in British pubs; 'a pint' alone usually means a pint of beer.
pragmatic_note: 'Going for a pint' often means a social drink, not necessarily just one.
pitfall: A British pint is larger than an American pint, which is 473 ml.
examples: Fancy a pint after work?
A pint of bitter and a glass of white wine, please.

gloss: Half a pint of beer or cider.
usage: Standard way to order a smaller drink in a British pub.
examples: Just a half for me, I'm driving.
A half of cider, please.

gloss: A traditional British amber-coloured ale, served at cellar temperature.
usage: Ordered in pubs as 'a pint of bitter'; associated with traditional pubs.
pitfall: It is not served ice-cold, and that is intentional, not a mistake.
examples: A pint of bitter, please.
This local bitter is brewed just down the road.

gloss: Traditional beer that finishes fermenting in the cask and is hand-pulled at the bar.
usage: Valued in traditional British pubs; promoted by CAMRA, the Campaign for Real Ale.
pragmatic_note: Real-ale enthusiasts have a slightly comic, beard-and-tankard stereotype in Britain.
examples: This pub has six real ales on tap.
He's really into real ale.

gloss: A pale, fizzy, cold beer, the most popular type in Britain.
usage: Standard pub word; Britons distinguish lager from ale and bitter.
pitfall: Ordering 'a beer' in Britain is vague; most people specify lager, ale or bitter.
examples: A pint of lager and a packet of crisps, please.
Is there an alcohol-free lager?

gloss: An alcoholic drink made from fermented apples.
usage: Very popular in British pubs, especially in the West Country.
pitfall: In the US 'cider' often means non-alcoholic apple juice; British cider is always alcoholic.
examples: A pint of cider, please.
Somerset is famous for its cider.

gloss: Beer mixed with lemonade, making a lighter, lower-alcohol drink.
usage: A traditional British pub drink, popular on summer days.
examples: I'll just have a shandy, I'm driving.
A lager shandy is perfect on a hot day.

gloss: A gin-based fruit liqueur, mixed with lemonade, fruit and mint as a summer drink.
usage: Associated with the British summer, Wimbledon, garden parties and regattas.
pragmatic_note: A jug of Pimm's signals a sunny British summer afternoon.
examples: Shall I make a jug of Pimm's for the garden?
Pimm's and strawberries are a Wimbledon tradition.

gloss: A gin and tonic.
usage: Widely used in British bars and homes as a casual abbreviation.
examples: I'll have a G&T, please.
A G&T in the garden after work is bliss.

gloss: Red wine heated with spices, sugar and orange, drunk in winter.
usage: Popular at Christmas markets and parties across Britain.
examples: Mulled wine and mince pies, anyone?
The Christmas market sells mulled wine.

gloss: Sparkling wine mixed with orange juice.
usage: Traditional at British celebration breakfasts, weddings and Christmas morning.
examples: We always have Buck's Fizz on Christmas morning.
A glass of Buck's Fizz to start the wedding breakfast.

gloss: Informal word for sparkling wine such as Champagne or prosecco.
usage: Common in British celebrations: 'a glass of fizz'.
examples: Shall we open a bottle of fizz?
There's fizz on arrival at the wedding.

gloss: Cheap, ordinary wine.
usage: Informal and humorous British word, often self-deprecating.
pragmatic_note: Calling your own wine 'plonk' is modest; calling a host's wine plonk is rude.
examples: It's only cheap plonk, I'm afraid.
We drank a bottle of plonk in the garden.

gloss: An unplanned or slightly naughty drink, usually during the day or after work.
usage: Very common in casual British speech among friends.
pitfall: Avoid in formal settings; 'cheeky' here means mildly indulgent, not rude.
examples: Fancy a cheeky pint after work?
We stopped for a cheeky pint on the way home.

gloss: A set of drinks bought by one person for everyone in the group.
usage: Central to British pub culture; people take turns buying rounds.
pragmatic_note: Not buying your round when it's your turn is a serious social faux pas in Britain.
examples: It's my round; what are you having?
Whose round is it?

gloss: The final chance to order drinks before a pub closes.
usage: Announced in British pubs, often with a bell.
examples: Last orders at the bar, please!
We got there just before last orders.

gloss: Your nearest or regular pub.
usage: Common British phrase: 'Shall we go to the local?'
pragmatic_note: Having a 'local' where staff know you is a cherished part of British life.
examples: We'll have a quick one at the local.
The local does a great Sunday roast.

gloss: An outdoor seating area at a pub.
usage: Hugely popular in Britain on the first sunny days of the year.
pragmatic_note: Britons pack beer gardens the moment the sun appears, whatever the temperature.
examples: Let's sit in the beer garden while it's sunny.
The beer garden was packed all afternoon.

gloss: In most British pubs, you go to the bar to order and pay instead of waiting for table service.
usage: Standard practice in British pubs, including for food.
pragmatic_note: Visitors often sit waiting for a waiter that never comes; check for a table number instead.
pitfall: Many pubs ask you to note your table number when ordering food at the bar.
examples: Do we order at the bar here?
You order at the bar and they bring the food over.

gloss: A small first course before the main meal.
usage: Standard term on British restaurant menus.
examples: Shall we share a starter?
I'll have the soup as a starter.

gloss: The principal dish of a meal, often called 'the main' or 'mains'.
usage: Standard term on British menus.
pitfall: In Britain an 'entrée' traditionally means a starter or side dish, not the main course.
examples: What are you having for your main?
The mains all come with seasonal veg.

gloss: The written total for a meal in a restaurant or café.
usage: Standard British term; 'Could we have the bill, please?'
pragmatic_note: In Britain you usually have to ask for the bill; staff may consider it rude to bring it unasked.
pitfall: Asking for 'the check' sounds American, and a 'cheque' is a bank payment.
examples: Could we have the bill, please?
Shall we split the bill?

gloss: An extra percentage added to a restaurant bill for staff, usually optional.
usage: Commonly added in British restaurants, especially for larger groups.
pragmatic_note: If service is already included, Britons usually leave no further tip.
pitfall: It is discretionary; you may politely ask for it to be removed if service was poor.
examples: Is service included?
There's a discretionary service charge on the bill.

gloss: To reserve a place at a restaurant in advance.
usage: Usual British phrasing; 'booking' is the noun.
examples: I've booked a table for eight o'clock.
Do you have a booking?

gloss: Hot food bought from a shop or restaurant to eat at home, or the shop itself.
usage: Standard British word; 'getting a takeaway' is a classic Friday night.
pitfall: Britons say 'takeaway' for both the food and the shop.
examples: Shall we just get a takeaway tonight?
There's a Chinese takeaway on the corner.

gloss: To eat your food inside a café or restaurant rather than take it away.
usage: Standard question in British cafés: 'Eat in or take away?'
pitfall: 'For here or to go?' sounds American; Britons ask 'eat in or take away?'
examples: Is that to eat in or take away?
We'll eat in, thanks.

gloss: An Indian meal or restaurant, as in 'going for an Indian'.
usage: Very common British usage; similarly 'a Chinese' or 'a Thai'; 'going for a curry' is a much-loved ritual.
pragmatic_note: Many 'Indian' restaurants in Britain are Bangladeshi- or Pakistani-run, with an Anglo-Indian menu.
examples: Shall we go for an Indian on Saturday?
Let's get an Indian delivered tonight.

gloss: A British-style Indian restaurant serving dishes like korma, madras and tikka masala.
usage: Found on almost every British high street.
pitfall: British curry-house dishes often differ from home cooking in South Asia.
examples: There's a great curry house on the high street.
Brick Lane is famous for its curry houses.

gloss: A fish and chip shop.
usage: Everyday British word; a Friday 'chippy tea' is a family tradition.
examples: Shall we get a chippy tonight?
The chippy round the corner does the best chips.

gloss: A small, cheap, unpretentious café serving fried breakfasts and tea.
usage: Affectionate British term for a no-frills café.
pragmatic_note: Calling a place a greasy spoon is usually fond, not an insult.
examples: There's a great greasy spoon by the station.
Nothing beats a fry-up at a proper greasy spoon.

gloss: An informal word for a cheap, simple café.
usage: Casual British speech, especially for an old-fashioned workers' café or roadside café.
pitfall: Not the same as a trendy coffee shop; a caff is cheap and basic.
examples: Let's grab a bacon sandwich at the caff.
The builders all eat at the caff on the corner.

gloss: A small café serving tea, cakes, scones and light lunches.
usage: Common in British villages, market towns and stately homes.
examples: Let's stop at the tearoom for a scone.
The village tearoom does lovely cream teas.

gloss: Simple, hearty food served in pubs.
usage: Informal British term for traditional pub meals.
examples: The pub does decent pub grub.
Fancy some pub grub tonight?

gloss: A pub that serves high-quality, restaurant-style food.
usage: Common British term since the 1990s.
examples: We booked a table at the new gastropub.
Gastropub food can be pricey.

gloss: A restaurant or buffet where roast meats are carved for you to order.
usage: A popular British pub and hotel offering, especially on Sundays.
examples: Let's go to the carvery for Sunday lunch.
The carvery has turkey, beef and gammon.

gloss: Knives, forks and spoons used for eating.
usage: Standard British term in homes and restaurants.
pitfall: Britons rarely say 'silverware' unless it's actually silver.
examples: The cutlery is on the side.
Could we have some clean cutlery, please?

gloss: A small square of cloth or paper for wiping your mouth and hands at meals.
usage: Used across Britain, though 'napkin' is also very common.
pragmatic_note: 'Serviette' has long been labelled lower-middle-class by snobbish commentators; 'napkin' is the safe choice.
examples: Could I have a serviette, please?
There are paper serviettes by the till.

gloss: A container with a handle and a lip for pouring water, milk or other liquids.
usage: Everyday British word in homes, pubs and restaurants.
examples: Could we have a jug of water for the table?
Put the milk in a jug.

gloss: A meal where people serve themselves from dishes laid out on a table.
usage: Pronounced 'BUFF-ay' in Britain, with the stress on the first syllable.
pitfall: Americans stress the second syllable: 'buh-FAY'.
examples: There's a buffet lunch after the ceremony.
Help yourself from the buffet.

gloss: Small snacks such as crisps, nuts and olives served with drinks.
usage: Common British word at parties and in pubs.
examples: Bring some nibbles for the party.
There are a few nibbles on the table.

gloss: Slightly hungry.
usage: Very common British word for a mild urge to eat.
examples: I'm feeling a bit peckish; is there any cake?
Grab a biscuit if you're peckish.

gloss: So tasty that you want to keep eating more.
usage: Very common British compliment for snacks and food.
pitfall: Pronounced 'MOR-ish'; it is not widely known outside Britain.
examples: These crisps are dangerously moreish.
Your flapjacks are really moreish.

gloss: Very full after eating.
usage: Common in casual British speech after a big meal.
examples: I couldn't eat another bite, I'm stuffed.
I'm stuffed; no pudding for me.

gloss: To start eating with enthusiasm.
usage: Common friendly invitation when food is served: 'Tuck in!'
examples: Tuck in before it gets cold!
The kids tucked into their pizza.

gloss: An informal word for food.
usage: Casual British speech; also 'a nosh-up' for a big meal.
examples: The nosh at that pub is excellent.
Let's have a proper nosh-up.

gloss: An informal word for food, especially simple hearty food.
usage: Common in casual British speech.
examples: The grub here is great.
Grub's up!

gloss: A small local shop selling groceries, newspapers, sweets and essentials.
usage: A familiar part of British neighbourhoods, often family-run.
pragmatic_note: Nipping to the corner shop for milk is an everyday British errand.
examples: I'll nip to the corner shop for some milk.
The corner shop is open until eleven.

gloss: A shop licensed to sell alcohol to take away.
usage: Standard British term, informally 'the offie'.
pitfall: Note the British spelling 'licence' for the noun.
examples: I'll pop to the off-licence for some wine.
The offie closes at ten.

gloss: A shop or shopkeeper selling fresh fruit and vegetables.
usage: Traditional British term, also 'the greengrocer's'.
examples: The greengrocer's on the high street has lovely strawberries.
I buy my veg from the local greengrocer.

gloss: A shop or person selling fresh fish.
usage: Standard British term, also 'the fishmonger's'.
examples: Ask the fishmonger to fillet it for you.
The fishmonger's has fresh crab today.

gloss: The main regular trip to buy household food.
usage: Very common British phrase: 'doing the weekly shop'.
pitfall: 'Shop' here is a noun meaning a shopping trip.
examples: I'll do the weekly shop on Saturday.
We get our weekly shop delivered.

gloss: A large wheeled basket used for shopping in supermarkets.
usage: Standard British word in supermarkets.
pragmatic_note: Many British supermarket trolleys need a coin or token to unlock them.
examples: Grab a trolley; we've got loads to buy.
Have you got a pound coin for the trolley?

gloss: The place in a shop where you pay.
usage: Standard British word: 'pay at the till'.
examples: Please pay at the till.
There's a massive queue at the tills.

gloss: A plastic or paper bag provided by shops for carrying purchases.
usage: Standard British term; shops in Britain charge for single-use bags.
examples: Do you need a carrier bag?
I forgot to bring my carrier bags.

gloss: A sturdy reusable shopping bag sold by supermarkets.
usage: Common British term since supermarkets started charging for bags.
examples: I've got a bag for life in the car.
Don't forget your bags for life.

gloss: Products sold under a supermarket's own name, usually cheaper.
usage: Common British term for supermarket-label goods.
examples: The own-brand cereal is just as good.
We switched to own brand to save money.

gloss: A lunchtime offer combining a sandwich, snack and drink for one fixed price.
usage: A British lunchtime institution in supermarkets and chemists.
pragmatic_note: Choosing the perfect meal deal combination is a popular British office topic.
examples: I'm just grabbing a meal deal for lunch.
What's your go-to meal deal?

gloss: A label marking reduced-price food near its use-by date in British supermarkets.
usage: Common British shopping talk; bargain hunters look for 'yellow-sticker' items.
examples: I got this salmon on yellow sticker.
The yellow stickers go on at about seven.

gloss: The date by which a shop should sell a product.
usage: Common British term, though 'use-by' and 'best before' are the official labels.
pitfall: Britons often say 'sell-by date' when they really mean the use-by date.
examples: This milk is past its sell-by date.
Check the sell-by date before you buy it.

gloss: The date after which food may be unsafe to eat.
usage: Official British food-label term, used on perishable foods.
pitfall: It is a safety date; 'best before' is only about quality.
examples: Don't eat it after the use-by date.
Check the use-by date on the chicken.

gloss: The date until which food is at its best quality.
usage: Official British label for longer-lasting foods; eating after it is usually safe.
examples: These biscuits are past their best before, but they're fine.
The best before date is on the lid.

gloss: A small plastic or cardboard container for soft fruit like strawberries.
usage: Standard British term in shops and markets.
examples: Two punnets of strawberries, please.
A punnet of raspberries for a pound.

gloss: A pre-cooked meal that only needs heating in the oven or microwave.
usage: Very common British term in supermarkets.
examples: I'll just have a ready meal tonight.
Ready meals are handy but often salty.

gloss: A sealed metal container for food; Britons say 'a tin of beans'.
usage: Standard British word for food containers; 'can' is used for drinks.
pitfall: Britons say 'a tin of tomatoes' but 'a can of cola'.
examples: Open a tin of chopped tomatoes.
There's a tin of beans in the cupboard.

gloss: A tool for opening tins of food.
usage: Standard British word in the kitchen.
examples: Where's the tin opener?
This tin has a ring pull, so you don't need the tin opener.

gloss: The flat top of a cooker with burners or rings for cooking in pans.
usage: Standard British term in kitchens and recipes.
examples: Leave the pan on the hob to simmer.
We've got an induction hob.

gloss: A kitchen appliance with an oven and a hob.
usage: Standard British term.
pitfall: In Britain a 'cooker' is an appliance; a 'cook' is a person.
examples: We need a new cooker.
Turn the cooker off when you're done.

gloss: To cook food under direct heat from above; also the part of the cooker that does this.
usage: Standard British term in recipes and kitchens.
pitfall: In Britain 'grill' means cooking under heat; Americans say 'broil' and use 'grill' for barbecuing.
examples: Grill the bacon until crisp.
Pop it under the grill for two minutes.

gloss: A padded glove for handling hot dishes.
usage: Standard British term.
examples: Use the oven gloves; that tray is boiling.
Where are the oven gloves?

gloss: A flat metal tray for baking food in the oven.
usage: Standard British term in recipes.
examples: Line the baking tray with greaseproof paper.
Spread the chips out on a baking tray.

gloss: A metal container for baking cakes.
usage: Standard British term; also a tin for storing cakes.
examples: Grease and line a 20 cm cake tin.
Pour the batter into the cake tin.

gloss: Paper that resists grease, used for lining tins and wrapping food.
usage: Standard British term in baking.
examples: Line the tin with greaseproof paper.
Wrap the sandwiches in greaseproof paper.

gloss: Thin, clear plastic film for covering food.
usage: Standard British term.
examples: Cover the bowl with cling film.
Wrap the dough in cling film.

gloss: Thin metal sheet for wrapping or covering food.
usage: Common British term; also 'kitchen foil' or 'aluminium foil'.
pitfall: British spelling and pronunciation is 'aluminium', with five syllables.
examples: Cover the turkey with tin foil.
Wrap the potatoes in tin foil.

gloss: Absorbent paper on a roll for kitchen use.
usage: Standard British term.
examples: Pass me some kitchen roll.
Drain the bacon on kitchen roll.

gloss: A mesh utensil for straining liquids or sifting flour.
usage: Standard British term.
pitfall: Pronounced 'siv', rhyming with 'give'.
examples: Pass the flour through a sieve.
Drain the peas in a sieve.

gloss: A device for weighing ingredients.
usage: Essential in British kitchens; recipes use grams.
pragmatic_note: Britons bake by weight, so American cup measurements can cause confusion.
examples: Weigh the flour on the kitchen scales.
Have you got digital kitchen scales?

gloss: A scale for setting the temperature of a gas oven.
usage: Common in British recipes alongside Celsius.
examples: Preheat the oven to 180 degrees, gas mark 4.
Bake at gas mark 6 for twenty minutes.

gloss: An oven with a fan to circulate hot air.
usage: Standard British term; recipes often give a lower 'fan' temperature.
examples: Reduce the temperature by 20 degrees for a fan oven.
Our fan oven cooks really evenly.

gloss: A small lump of butter.
usage: Common in British recipes and cooking talk.
examples: Add a knob of butter to the pan.
Finish the sauce with a knob of butter.

gloss: To cut off both ends of a vegetable or fruit.
usage: Common British cooking term for beans and gooseberries.
examples: Top and tail the green beans.
Can you top and tail the gooseberries?

gloss: A crumbly pastry made from flour, fat and water.
usage: Standard British pastry for pies and tarts.
examples: I'll make shortcrust pastry for the quiche.
You can buy ready-rolled shortcrust pastry.

gloss: Very thin sheets of pastry used in layered dishes.
usage: Standard British spelling in shops and recipes.
examples: Brush the filo sheets with butter.
Filo pastry dries out quickly, so keep it covered.
